title: Migration Planning: Assessment, Strategies, Dependencies, and Licensing
bodyMarkdown:
## The migration journey

Google's [migration framework](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/migration-to-gcp-getting-started) has four phases:

1. **Assess**: understand inventory, dependencies, costs and performance baselines.
2. **Plan**: design the cloud foundation (resource hierarchy, identity, networking) and prioritize workloads.
3. **Deploy**: move workloads and data to Google Cloud. Older material calls this "migrate"; the framework names it deploy.
4. **Optimize**: use cloud capabilities to improve performance, scalability and cost after the move.

Most failed migrations skipped rigorous assessment: an undiscovered dependency, an unlicensed product, or a workload that did not need to move at all. On the exam, when a scenario describes an organization about to migrate with no inventory, the answer is almost always an assessment step, not a migration step.

## Assess: inventory, dependencies, TCO

The [assessment phase guidance](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/migration-to-gcp-assessing-and-discovering-your-workloads) asks you to build a complete workload inventory including dependencies, supporting services and hardware appliances, and to record facts such as where the source code lives and whether you can modify it, plus licensing requirements for software and hardware. Workloads are then placed in a catalog matrix using criteria such as business criticality, dependencies, tolerance for downtime and migration complexity. Criticality ratings run from workloads that tolerate no downtime to those that tolerate up to 48 hours in the guide's example, and complexity is rated easy, hard or cannot-move. The guide also tells you to run proofs of concept, to compute total cost of ownership including on-premises operating costs such as power, cooling and maintenance, and to validate feasibility before committing.

**Migration Center** is the tool built for this phase. According to the [Migration Center overview](https://cloud.google.com/migration-center/docs/migration-center-overview) it is a unified platform to estimate costs, scan and assess infrastructure and plan the migration without changing your workloads. It can:

- Discover and inventory servers and Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL and PostgreSQL databases, from on-premises and other clouds, using a discovery client, a discovery client CLI for one-time exports, or manual import.
- Identify application and network dependencies so you know which components must move together.
- Produce TCO reports driven by your migration preferences and technical fit assessments for Google Cloud products.
- Provide planning best practices and recommendations for what to migrate.

Pick first movers carefully. The assessment guide recommends workloads with the fewest dependencies and minimal refactoring needs, which builds team skills with low risk.

Distractors in this area are build and deploy tools such as Cloud Build, Cloud Deploy and Config Connector. None of them inventories or assesses a source estate.

## Migration strategies

The framework lists six migration types, ordered here from least to most effort:

| Strategy | What you do | Effort | Choose when |
|----------|-------------|--------|-------------|
| **Rehost** (lift and shift) | Move with minor or no changes, VM to VM | Lowest | Deadline pressure, little business case for change; modernize later |
| **Replatform** (lift and optimize) | Move with targeted improvements to gain elasticity or redundancy, such as a managed database instead of a self-run one | Moderate | Quick wins are available without redesigning the app |
| **Refactor** (move and improve) | Modify the workload to exploit cloud capabilities | High | The architecture is unsupported as-is or needs major updates |
| **Re-architect** (modernize) | Restructure, for example into microservices | Very high | Long-term agility and scale justify more complexity and testing |
| **Rebuild** (remove and replace) | Redesign and rewrite as a fully cloud-optimized app | Highest | The app no longer meets goals or is too costly to migrate otherwise |
| **Repurchase** | Replace an on-premises product with its SaaS equivalent | Varies | A suitable SaaS exists |

Two portfolio dispositions sit beside the migration types: **retire** (decommission what is unneeded, duplicated or unsupported) and **retain** (leave in place for now because of constraints or readiness). They are common in build, buy, modify or deprecate analysis and in exam questions. An internal app that duplicates a SaaS the company already pays for, has few users and high maintenance cost is a retire (deprecate) decision, not something to refactor or rehost. The cheapest migration is the one you do not do.

## Dependency and network planning

- Build the dependency map first and move tightly coupled components in the same wave. Splitting a chatty application across the on-premises to cloud link produces latency and egress costs.
- Plan IP address ranges across on-premises and every VPC before connecting them; overlapping ranges make routing ambiguous and are very costly to fix later.
- Choose hybrid connectivity from the [connectivity guide](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/how-to/choose-product): HA VPN is quick to set up and offers a 99.99% or 99.9% SLA depending on topology; Dedicated Interconnect gives 10, 100 or 400 Gbps circuits with VLAN attachments from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps; Partner Interconnect provides 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps attachments through a service provider; Cross-Cloud Interconnect links to other clouds. A common pattern is VPN first to start, Interconnect for sustained high-volume transfer and low latency.

### Landing zone: Shared VPC and hybrid routing

**Shared VPC.** Per the [Shared VPC documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc), a host project contains the shared network and service projects attach to it. A project cannot be both host and service project, each service project attaches to only one host, and all must be in the same organization. Network administration is centralized (Shared VPC Admin attaches projects, Network Admin manages network resources except firewalls) while each team keeps its own project, IAM and budget. Choose Shared VPC for one organization with a central network team and many application teams; choose VPC Network Peering or Private Service Connect to join independently administered networks. Some existing resources must be re-created to use it, so decide before the waves begin.

**Cloud Router and BGP.** [Cloud Router](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/overview) is the BGP speaker that creates dynamic routes from on-premises prefixes. It is control plane only (packets are forwarded by Google's network virtualization, not by Cloud Router) and is required for HA VPN, every Interconnect type and router appliances. Its [dynamic routing mode](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/router/concepts/learned-routes) matters for migrations: in regional mode each region uses only routes learned in that region, so a VPN or Interconnect in one region leaves workloads in other regions with no path on-premises; global mode propagates the best paths to every region, adding an inter-region cost to MED when `bgpInterRegionCost` is `ADD_COST_TO_MED`. Subnet routes take precedence over static and dynamic routes, then the most specific destination wins, then priority (default 1000) among [routes](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/routes).

## Moving data

Match the tool to the data type and size.

| Need | Tool | Key facts |
|------|------|-----------|
| Large file or object datasets from S3, Azure Blob, on-premises file systems, HDFS or HTTP sources | **[Storage Transfer Service](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/overview)** | One-time or recurring; optimized for more than 1 TiB; on-premises sources use self-hosted agents; no SLA on transfer performance |
| Data too large or too slow to push over the network | **[Transfer Appliance](https://cloud.google.com/transfer-appliance/docs/4.0/overview)** | Offline; consider when upload would take more than a week; example: 300 TB at 100 Mbps takes about 9 months, versus under 25 days to fill the appliance, then about 10 more business days to appear in Cloud Storage |
| Operational databases with low downtime | **[Database Migration Service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview)** | Homogeneous and heterogeneous, relational engines only (sources and destinations in the matrix below); continuous jobs use change data capture (CDC) after an initial snapshot, one-time jobs may involve downtime |
| Ongoing change replication into analytics | **[Datastream](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/overview)** | Serverless CDC from databases such as MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and MongoDB into BigQuery or Cloud Storage |

Choose a continuous Database Migration Service job when the business cannot tolerate a long outage at cutover: the source stays online while changes are replicated, and you promote the destination when it is synchronized. Choose a one-time job only for small or non-critical databases where downtime is acceptable.

### Database migration tooling matrix

Database Migration Service (DMS) supports homogeneous migrations (MySQL to Cloud SQL for MySQL; PostgreSQL to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL or AlloyDB; SQL Server to Cloud SQL for SQL Server) and heterogeneous ones (Oracle or SQL Server to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB for PostgreSQL), per the [overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/database-migration/docs/overview). Heterogeneous jobs use a conversion workspace for schema and code. Redis and MongoDB are not listed sources and have their own paths.

| Source | Path | Catch |
|--------|------|-------|
| MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle | DMS to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB (targets above) | Heterogeneous needs schema and code conversion |
| MongoDB | [Datastream plus Dataflow](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/migrate-data) into Firestore with MongoDB compatibility (Enterprise edition) | MongoDB 4.0 or later as a replica set or sharded cluster (Change Streams); a short write outage at cutover |
| Redis | Export an RDB file to Cloud Storage and [import it](https://docs.cloud.google.com/memorystore/docs/redis/import-data) into Memorystore for Redis | Import overwrites all instance data and the instance is unavailable meanwhile; only older-version backups import |

Datastream writes directly to BigQuery and Cloud Storage; reaching Cloud SQL or Spanner takes [Dataflow templates](https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/overview). DMS moves the database; Datastream feeds analytics.

### Data warehouse modernization

[BigQuery Migration Service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/migration-intro) covers assessment, SQL translation to GoogleSQL (batch translator, interactive translator, translation API) and data transfer, for sources such as Teradata, Oracle and Exadata, Snowflake, Redshift, Netezza and Hadoop or Hive. [BigQuery Data Transfer Service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/dts-introduction) is the scheduled, managed loader for supported sources (Cloud Storage, S3, Azure Blob, Teradata, Redshift, SaaS applications), with backfill. Before decommissioning the source, run the open-source [Data Validation Tool](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/migration/migration-overview) to prove source and destination tables match. Re-hosting a warehouse engine on VMs carries the old operations along, and Bare Metal Solution is transitioning to allowlist-only, so neither is a default answer.

### Mainframe modernization

Google's [mainframe overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/mainframe-assessment-tool/docs/mainframe-modernization-overview) maps tools to three phases. **Assess** with Mainframe Assessment Tool (dependencies, business logic, scope); **modernize** with Antigravity (code transformation and generation) and Mainframe Connector (data conversion and migration); **validate** with [Dual Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/mainframe-dual-run/docs/dual-run-overview), which runs the mainframe and the Google Cloud version side by side on the same inputs, can replay live production events, and flags output differences. Cut over when the two are equivalent.

## Licensing planning

Licensing is a first-class TCO input. The [Microsoft licensing guide](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/windows/ms-licensing) describes two models on Compute Engine:

- **On-demand (pay-as-you-go)**: pay for Microsoft licenses through Google Cloud, only for the resources you consume, using prebuilt images for Windows Server and SQL Server. No upfront investment and no separate licensing agreement to manage. Autoscaled instances are charged for the time they run; nothing is repurchased on each scale event.
- **Bring your own license (BYOL)**: reuse eligible licenses and pay only for compute. Eligibility paths include Software Assurance with License Mobility, for application server licenses such as SQL Server and SharePoint Server, which requires an existing Microsoft Volume Licensing agreement with active Software Assurance. Software acquired through Outsourcing Software Management Rights (available for certain products released before October 1, 2019) can only be used on dedicated servers such as sole-tenant nodes.

[Sole-tenant nodes](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/nodes/sole-tenant-nodes) are physical Compute Engine servers dedicated to hosting only your project's VMs. They report the physical server ID for each VM, which supports per-core or per-processor license tracking, and they also serve security isolation and performance isolation needs. You define node templates (regional, immutable properties), node groups (zonal collections of identical nodes) and node types such as n2-node-80-640, which provides 80 vCPUs and 640 GB of memory per node. Host maintenance runs on a multi-week cycle with three policy choices, and the dedicated hardware carries a premium. Verify every licensing situation with legal or your Microsoft vendor.

**Decision rule.** The [Microsoft licensing FAQ](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/windows/ms-licensing-faq) sorts BYOL by rights. SQL Server with active Software Assurance and License Mobility can run on default multi-tenant VMs. Without Software Assurance it comes only to sole-tenant nodes, and only if it meets the Outsourcing Software Management Rights criteria. Windows Server is not covered by License Mobility, and per-core Windows Server licensing exists only on sole-tenant nodes. Committed use discounts cover vCPU and memory; the documented license commitments apply only to SLES, SLES for SAP and RHEL images, so a compute commitment does not lower Windows Server or SQL Server license charges.

### Specialized and isolation-sensitive workloads

| Requirement | Choose | Key facts |
|-------------|--------|-----------|
| Data protected while in use, such as regulated analytics | **[Confidential VM](https://cloud.google.com/confidential-computing/confidential-vm/docs/about-cvm)** | Hardware memory encryption (AMD SEV, SEV-SNP, Intel TDX; NVIDIA for GPUs); SEV overhead ranges from none to minimal; live migration only for AMD SEV on N2D and C3D |
| Hypervisor-free access: third-party hypervisors, hardware counters, licensing that forbids virtualization | **[Bare metal instances](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/bare-metal-instances)** | Offered on series such as C3, C4, X4 and X5; a single network interface |
| Physical isolation or per-core license tracking | **Sole-tenant nodes** | Dedicated host, you pay a premium |
| SAP HANA | **SAP-certified memory-optimized types** | Only a subset of machine types is [certified](https://cloud.google.com/sap/docs/certifications-sap-hana); M-series VMs, and X4 and X5 bare metal up to 32 TB and 49 TB |

Confidential VM encrypts memory against the host; sole-tenancy keeps other customers off your hardware. Neither implies the other.

## Incremental modernization: the strangler fig

Rehost and replatform move a workload as one unit. When a monolith cannot be replaced in a single cutover and the business cannot freeze features while you rebuild, use the [strangler fig pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/strangler-fig) (vendor-neutral; Google Cloud products supply the facade). A facade intercepts every request and routes it to the legacy system or to a new service. You move one capability at a time, shift traffic gradually, and retire the legacy part when it receives no traffic.

| Facade | How it routes | Fits |
|--------|---------------|------|
| **External Application Load Balancer** URL map with a [hybrid connectivity NEG](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/negs/hybrid-neg-concepts) | Host and path rules, plus [weighted backend services](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/https/traffic-management-global) (for example 95% old, 5% new); the hybrid NEG points at the on-premises IP:port over VPN or Interconnect, while Cloud Run or GKE backends serve the new routes | HTTP traffic with a legacy backend reachable over hybrid connectivity; the NEG needs Cloud Router in global dynamic routing mode |
| **Apigee** API proxy | [Conditional route rules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/fundamentals/understanding-routes) choose among target endpoints; [proxies decouple the app-facing API from backends](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/fundamentals/understanding-apis-and-api-proxies) | A governed API program with consumers you do not control, keys, quotas and analytics |

**Sequence.**

1. Put the facade in front, routing 100% to legacy, with no behavior change.
2. Pick one capability with a clear boundary and few dependencies and build it on Cloud Run or GKE.
3. Send a small share to it and compare error rate and latency with the baselines from assessment.
4. Raise the share to 100%. Rollback is a routing change, not a redeploy.
5. When the legacy component gets zero traffic, delete it; when nothing is left, decommission the legacy system and optionally remove the facade.

**Data during the overlap.** Both systems need consistent data. Keep the legacy database as the system of record at first, then give each new service its own store, replicated from the legacy one with change data capture (Database Migration Service continuous jobs or Datastream, above). Validate consistency, make the new store authoritative, and delete the legacy tables last, because rollback gets expensive once they are gone.

| Alternative | Why it fails when you cannot cut over once or freeze features |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Big-bang rewrite** | One high-risk cutover and a feature freeze while it is built |
| **Containerize the whole monolith** | A rehost: it still deploys and fails as one unit and decomposes nothing |
| **Design every service first** | Delays all value and assumes you already know the boundaries |

**When a facade is not the answer.** The pattern needs a point where requests can be intercepted. It is a poor fit for a small, simple system that is easier to replace outright, or when the data center exit date demands a fast, full decommission (rehost first, modernize later). The facade itself must be highly available.

## Cutover and optimization

1. Migrate in waves, starting with low-dependency, low-risk workloads.
2. Validate functionality and NFRs (latency, throughput, error rate) against the baselines captured during assessment.
3. Keep rollback available, then decommission source systems on a schedule so you stop paying twice.
4. Optimize: right-size from observed utilization, apply committed use discounts or Spot where suitable, and move rehosted components to managed services over time.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Skipping assessment** and discovering dependencies during cutover.
- **Rehosting everything,** including applications that should be retired or replaced with SaaS.
- **Refactoring for its own sake** when a deadline or low business value calls for rehost now, modernize later.
- **Splitting dependent services across waves,** leaving them separated by a slow link.
- **Transferring petabytes over a modest link** when Transfer Appliance fits, or shipping an appliance for a few hundred gigabytes that Storage Transfer Service handles online.
- **One-time database migration for a 24/7 system** instead of continuous replication.
- **Ignoring licenses** that require dedicated hardware or lack mobility rights, which surface as audit findings after the move.
- **Regional dynamic routing with a single-region link** to a multi-region VPC, leaving other regions without a path on-premises.
- **Forcing special workloads onto standard VMs:** SAP HANA on an uncertified machine type, or a hypervisor on a VM when bare metal is needed.
- **Overlapping IP ranges** discovered after ordering connectivity.
- **A big-bang rewrite or one-unit containerization** for a monolith that cannot take a single cutover or a feature freeze; use a routing facade and move one capability at a time.
- **The wrong database tool:** Datastream as a Cloud SQL migration path, DMS for Redis or MongoDB, or an RDB import into a Redis instance still serving traffic.
- **Declaring a warehouse migrated without validation,** or cutting over a mainframe without a parallel run.
- **A strangler facade as a single point of failure,** or retiring legacy tables before the new store is validated.
- **Treating the move as the end.** Without the optimize phase, rehosted estates tend to cost more than planned.

## Exam tips

- **Assessment and TCO is Migration Center.** Inventory, dependency mapping and TCO before migration; Cloud Build, Cloud Deploy and Config Connector are distractors.
- **Map the wording to the strategy.** As-is to meet a deadline is rehost; small cloud improvements is replatform; redesign for cloud-native is refactor or re-architect; SaaS replacement is repurchase.
- **Duplicated, low-use, high-maintenance means retire.** Do not refactor or rehost an app you no longer need.
- **Offline versus online.** If network upload would take more than about a week, think Transfer Appliance; for recurring or cloud-to-cloud object moves, Storage Transfer Service.
- **Minimal-downtime database cutover is Database Migration Service continuous mode** (CDC); Datastream is for ongoing replication into analytics targets (BigQuery or Cloud Storage) and never migrates a database into Cloud SQL.
- **DMS sources are MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle.** MongoDB goes to Firestore with MongoDB compatibility through Datastream and Dataflow; Redis through an RDB export and Memorystore import, which overwrites data.
- **Warehouse moves use BigQuery Migration Service** (assessment, SQL translation, transfer) and the Data Validation Tool to prove tables match. Mainframes: assess, modernize, then validate with Dual Run.
- **Two licensing facts.** Pay-as-you-go images for Windows Server and SQL Server simplify compliance, and sole-tenant nodes serve BYOL that requires dedicated hardware; licensing always affects TCO.
- **Shared VPC for central network control, peering or PSC across independent administrators.** Cloud Router (BGP) is control plane only; global dynamic routing mode makes one region's link reachable from every region.
- **Match isolation to the requirement.** Data in use means Confidential VM, hypervisor-free or non-virtualized licensing means bare metal, per-core license tracking means sole-tenant, and SAP HANA means a certified memory-optimized type.
- **No single cutover and no feature freeze means a strangler fig:** a routing facade (Apigee, or an external Application Load Balancer URL map with a hybrid NEG) in front, one capability at a time moved to Cloud Run or GKE, gradual traffic shift, rollback by routing, legacy retired at zero traffic.
- **Keep data in sync during the overlap** with change data capture, and delete legacy data last.
- **Sequence waves by dependency map** and pick low-dependency, low-refactoring first movers.
- **Use Interconnect for sustained high bandwidth and low latency, HA VPN for quick start,** and plan non-overlapping ranges up front.
